pr.title: coverage: Don't instrument `#[automatically_derived]` functions
pr.description:
This PR makes the coverage instrumentor detect and skip functions that have [`#[automatically_derived]`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/derive.html#the-automatically_derived-attribute) on their enclosing impl block.

Most notably, this means that methods generated by built-in derives (e.g. `Clone`, `Debug`, `PartialEq`) are now ignored by coverage instrumentation, and won't appear as executed or not-executed in coverage reports.

This is a noticeable change in user-visible behaviour, but overall I think it's a net improvement. For example, we've had a few user requests for this sort of change (e.g. #105055, https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/84605#issuecomment-1902069040), and I believe it's the behaviour that most users will expect/prefer by default.

It's possible to imagine situations where users would want to instrument these derived implementations, but I think it's OK to treat that as an opportunity to consider adding more fine-grained option flags to control the details of coverage instrumentation, while leaving this new behaviour as the default.

(Also note that while `-Cinstrument-coverage` is a stable feature, the exact details of coverage instrumentation are allowed to change. So we *can* make this change; the main question is whether we *should*.)

Fixes #105055.

issues.title: Code coverage showing [derive(Debug)] as missed region

processing.reason: The historical change is a coverage-instrumentation eligibility decision, not a value-semantics rewrite. The pre-fix compiler instruments methods whose enclosing impl is `#[automatically_derived]`; the fix skips them when building coverage mappings/counters. Adding or omitting coverage counters does not change any function's arguments, return value, control flow, or deterministic side effects. Consequently, for any concrete input, the derived method (e.g. `<Foo as Debug>::fmt` or `<Foo as PartialEq>::eq`) produces the same value whether or not it was instrumented. The only observable difference is in coverage metadata (`.cov-map` function entries and `.coverage` counts/caret markers), which is compiler diagnostic output rather than a runtime value that the test harness can print. Any pair of ordinary Rust functions that returned different values here would have to invent an artificial "coverage happened" signal or alter the derived impl's behavior, which would not encode the actual historical transformation. Therefore no source-grounded pair can satisfy the required criterion of different original/transformed runtime values.

analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically incorrect transformation is coverage instrumentation of a method whose enclosing impl block is `#[automatically_derived]` (for example, methods generated by built-in derives). This caused derive-generated implementations to receive coverage counters/mappings and appear as executed or not-executed in coverage reports, instead of being ignored. The corrected transformation is to skip such functions entirely when deciding whether to instrument them.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust functions compiled with coverage instrumentation (`-Cinstrument-coverage`) that are methods of an impl block marked `#[automatically_derived]`, especially impls generated by built-in derives such as `#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]`. The behavior concerns derived methods (used or unused, e.g. `clone`, `fmt`, `eq`, `cmp`, `partial_cmp`), not ordinary free functions and not manually written impl methods unless that impl itself is marked `#[automatically_derived]`. The changed tests cover structs/enums with derives and also doctest coverage.
analysis.originalLogic: `is_eligible_for_coverage` allowed a method to be instrumented based on ordinary eligibility checks, without considering whether the method's enclosing impl block came from a derive. In the pre-fix code the relevant added check was absent; the PR adds it between the existing early-return checks and the `NO_COVERAGE` check: `if let Some(impl_of) = tcx.impl_of_method(def_id.to_def_id()) && tcx.is_automatically_derived(impl_of) { ... return false; }`. Thus the original logic would instrument derived methods such as `<Foo as core::fmt::Debug>::fmt` and `<Foo as core::cmp::PartialEq>::eq`, as shown by the removed entries in the old `.cov-map` expectations.
pitfalls: Do not exclude all impl methods: only methods whose enclosing impl is `#[automatically_derived]` should be skipped.
Do not rely only on the derive attribute on the type; the patch checks `is_automatically_derived(impl_of)` on the impl block returned by `impl_of_method`.

Coverage output includes both per-function entries in `.cov-map` and line-level counts in `.coverage`; the historical tests show both must change (removed derived-function mapping blocks and removal of counts/caret annotations on derive lines).
Derived methods may be unused; old expectations included derived functions marked `(unused)` and still mapped, so tests should cover unused derived methods as well as used ones.
The check must not break other eligibility exclusions such as `#[coverage(off)]`; the PR also adds a trace message for the existing `NO_COVERAGE` branch but leaves that exclusion behavior intact.
This is a deliberate user-visible behavior change: derived impls no longer appear as executed or not-executed, rather than being reported as covered.
preconditions: The crate is compiled with coverage instrumentation enabled (the PR describes `-Cinstrument-coverage` as a stable feature).
The function under consideration is a method, so `tcx.impl_of_method(def_id.to_def_id())` yields the enclosing impl.
The enclosing impl block is marked `#[automatically_derived]`; the PR specifically describes built-in derives such as `Clone`, `Debug`, and `PartialEq` as the common source.
No earlier eligibility check has already excluded the function (the new check is added after earlier early-return checks and before the `NO_COVERAGE` check).
analysis.summary: Historical coverage-instrumentation eligibility bug: functions in `#[automatically_derived]` impl blocks (notably built-in `derive(Clone/Debug/PartialEq/...)` methods) were treated as normal eligible functions and instrumented, so derived methods appeared in coverage output as executed or missed. The fix in `InstrumentCoverage` detects the enclosing impl via `impl_of_method` + `is_automatically_derived` and excludes those functions from instrumentation.
analysis.testStrategy: Use the coverage test harness with source files containing a type whose derived impl methods would previously be instrumented (e.g. `#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)] struct Foo(u32);` or the broader `#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)] pub struct Version`). Compare the two transformations while keeping the Rust source identical: (A) eligibility treats derived methods as instrumentable, yielding function entries such as `<Foo as core::fmt::Debug>::fmt` / `<Foo as core::cmp::PartialEq>::eq` in `.cov-map` and counts/caret markers on the derive line in `.coverage`; (B) the corrected eligibility skips methods whose impl is `automatically_derived`, so those function mapping blocks are absent and the derive line has no execution count. Include both used and unused derived methods, and a manually written impl or free function as a control that should still be instrumented. The patch also adjusts `coverage-run-rustdoc/doctest.coverage`, so a doctest case with `#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]` is a worthwhile additional scenario. Inspect expected `.cov-map` and `.coverage` files; no compiler execution is claimed here.
analysis.trigger: A source file contains a type with a built-in derive (or another `#[automatically_derived]` impl), and coverage instrumentation considers the generated methods for instrumentation. The historical behavior manifests whenever those derived methods are present in coverage maps/reports; the issue example reports a derived enum with `#[derive(PartialEq, Debug)]` and expects 100% coverage but observes the derived `Debug` implementation shown as a missed region.
